passage: Everyone in this office calls me Manoj bhai now, Siddharth, but when I arrived in Dubai at twenty-four, nobody called me anything. What changed it wasn't one big thing. I found a tiny Kerala tea shop near the metro and went every morning at seven, same seat. After a month the owner poured my tea before I asked. I joined the Friday cricket in the park, bad batsman, loyal fielder. I learned to say shukran properly and to wait for the call to prayer to finish before phoning clients. And every Sunday I still made my mother's sambar, even when it tasted wrong. Those small things held me up while friendships took their time. So pick your tea shop, Siddharth. Pick your Sunday dish. The rest comes.

qa.q: What did Manoj make every Sunday?
qa.a: His mother's sambar, even when it tasted wrong.

qa.q: How can you tell the tea shop made Manoj feel he belonged?
qa.a: He went every morning to the same seat and still remembers the owner pouring his tea before he asked, a sign of finally being known.

qa.q: What does Manoj advise Siddharth to do?
qa.a: Pick a regular place and keep a ritual from home, like a tea shop and a Sunday dish, so there is steadiness while friends slowly form.

qa.q: What might Siddharth take from hearing that Manoj once felt unknown too?
qa.a: Siddharth may feel less alone in the first month, seeing that even the well-known Manoj bhai started out as a stranger.

grounding: Shows building roots through a regular tea shop, a sports group, local customs and a home ritual, which give steadiness while ties form.

passage: Night shifts at the warehouse in Brampton made routines hard, and the January snow made them harder. Gurpreet, twenty-five and eight months into Canada, slept while the street was awake. Still, she had built three things. Every Tuesday, snow or not, she walked to the gurdwara for the morning langar and stayed to help wash the big steel pots. Every Thursday she met Nirmala, a retired teacher from the ground floor, at the library's conversation hour, where they swapped words: Gurpreet taught a little Punjabi, and Nirmala taught winter ones like slush, black ice and toque. And every night before her shift she braided her hair the way her bebe had taught her, humming the same old song. This week the storm closed the library. So Nirmala knocked on her door with a flask of tea instead, and they practised in the corridor.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet do every Tuesday?
qa.a: She walked to the gurdwara for the morning langar and stayed to help wash the big steel pots.

qa.q: What does braiding her hair the way her bebe taught her suggest about Gurpreet?
qa.a: It suggests she draws comfort and steadiness from keeping a piece of home alive inside her new life.

qa.q: How did Gurpreet keep her routines going despite night shifts and snow?
qa.a: She tied them to fixed days rather than fixed places, so when the library closed, the practice simply moved to the corridor.

qa.q: What might the Thursday meetings mean to Nirmala?
qa.a: For Nirmala, retired and living downstairs, they may be a welcome friendship, which is why the tea arrived when the library shut 😊

grounding: Illustrates building routines and roots abroad through a community place, a new friendship and a ritual from home, despite night shifts and a snowstorm.

passage:
Six months after moving from Ludhiana to Chennai, Neelam had a Saturday that almost looked like a life.

At seven she walked to the same corner stall for filter coffee. The owner now poured it without asking and scolded her in Tamil for skipping last week. She answered, badly, in Tamil, and he laughed.

At ten she went to the yoga class near the beach, where she knew three names now.

In the evening she took the bus to the gurdwara in T. Nagar, as she'd done every Sunday at home with her grandmother. There she met Gurpreet, who ran a bakery in Anna Nagar and asked if she wanted to help with the langar next month.

Back in her flat, Neelam lit the small diya her mother had packed, and ate curd rice. Both things felt right.

qa.q: Where did Neelam go in the evening?
qa.a: She took the bus to the gurdwara in T. Nagar.

qa.q: What was Neelam feeling as she lit the diya and ate curd rice?
qa.a: She felt settled and content, with both her home ritual and her new habits feeling right together.

qa.q: What small step could deepen Neelam's roots further?
qa.a: Saying yes to helping with the langar would give her a regular role and new ties with Gurpreet and others.

qa.q: How might the coffee stall owner see Neelam now?
qa.a: He seems to see her as a regular he's fond of, teasing her for skipping a week and enjoying her attempts at Tamil.

grounding: A young woman builds steadiness in a new city through a regular café, a class, a faith community and home rituals, while new ties form.

passage:
"Same as usual?" Chandrika asked from behind the counter.

"Same as usual," said Omkar, and felt oddly pleased that there was a usual.

"Two months now," she said, pouring the coffee. "You came in the first week looking like someone had stolen your dog."

"I felt like it. Bengaluru was a lot."

"And now?"

"Now I have a gym at six, your coffee at seven, work, and cricket in the park on Sundays with the guys from the next building." He tapped the table. "And my Aai's poha on Wednesdays. I make it myself. Terribly."

Chandrika laughed. "You should bring some. I'll trade you a coffee."

"Deal. And, Chandrika, what's 'swalpa adjust maadi'? The auto driver keeps saying it."

"It means 'adjust a little.'" She grinned. "It's the whole city's advice."

qa.q: What does Omkar make on Wednesdays?
qa.a: Omkar makes his Aai's poha on Wednesdays.

qa.q: What was Omkar feeling when he realised he had a 'usual'?
qa.a: He felt pleased and more at home, a sign that his routines were giving him steadiness.

qa.q: What could Omkar try next to keep building roots?
qa.a: He could keep learning local phrases and take up Chandrika's offer to trade poha for coffee, turning a routine into a friendship.

qa.q: How does Chandrika see the change in Omkar?
qa.a: Chandrika sees a lost-looking newcomer who has become a relaxed regular, and she seems glad to be part of that.

grounding: A dialogue shows a newcomer steadied by a regular café, gym and sport, learning local ways and keeping a home ritual.

passage:
When I first came to Dubai for the engineering job, my weekends were a hole. I'm Pranav, and I lasted about two months of sleeping till noon and scrolling before I decided to build something like a week.

I found a small cricket club that played on Friday mornings in a dusty ground near Al Quoz. I found a Kerala restaurant where the owner started saving me the last parotta. I learned to say thank you in Arabic and started saying it to the watchman every morning.

Some things I brought with me. Every Sunday night I call my grandmother, and I still light an agarbatti by the window before work, the way we did at home.

Joseph, my flatmate from Manila, laughed at the agarbatti at first. Now he asks for one when he has an exam. The week has a shape. That shape holds me up.

qa.q: Where did the cricket club play?
qa.a: It played on Friday mornings in a dusty ground near Al Quoz.

qa.q: What was Pranav feeling in those first two months of weekends?
qa.a: Pranav felt empty and adrift, which pushed Pranav to build a routine.

qa.q: Which choices made the biggest difference for Pranav, and why?
qa.a: Joining the cricket club and becoming a regular at the restaurant gave regular contact, while the Sunday call and agarbatti kept a link to home.

qa.q: How has Joseph's view of the agarbatti changed?
qa.a: Joseph first laughed at it but now asks for one before exams, showing he has come to value the ritual too.

grounding: A first-person account shows a newcomer abroad building steadiness through clubs, a regular eatery, local phrases and rituals from home.

passage:
Note by Siddharth, team lead, three months after Anirban joined our Chennai office
When Anirban arrived from Kolkata in March, he ate at his desk and left at six sharp. I've noticed a real change since. He now goes to the same small café on Kutchery Road every morning; the owner starts his filter coffee when he walks in. He joined the office badminton group on Tuesdays and Fridays. He's learning Tamil phrases from our receptionist and practises them on the auto drivers, who seem to enjoy correcting him. On Sundays, he told me, he still makes luchi and aloo dum the way his mother does, and video-calls home while he eats. He seems steadier at work too, speaking up more in reviews.
What I did next: I asked him to show the two new joiners from Delhi around next week, since he knows now what the first month feels like.

qa.q: On which days does Anirban play badminton?
qa.a: He plays with the office badminton group on Tuesdays and Fridays.

qa.q: How does Anirban seem to feel now compared with March?
qa.a: Anirban seems steadier and more settled, relaxed enough to speak up more at work and enjoy practising Tamil.

qa.q: Which routines have helped Anirban, and why?
qa.a: A regular café, badminton twice a week, learning local phrases and keeping his Sunday luchi ritual from home give steady rhythms while new ties grow.

qa.q: How might the two new joiners from Delhi experience Anirban's help?
qa.a: They may feel welcomed and reassured, having someone who remembers how the first month feels to guide them around.

grounding: Shows a newcomer finding a regular café and sports group, learning local ways and keeping home rituals, building steadiness while new ties form.
